questions.question: What is the main objective of the Selection Sort algorithm?
options: To split an array into two halves
To put a list in order from smallest to biggest by repeatedly choosing the smallest item
To search for a specific target element in a sorted list
To pair up adjacent elements and swap them if they are out of order
questions.explanation: Selection Sort repeatedly scans the unsorted list for the minimum element and moves it into its sorted position.

questions.question: What is the overall Big-O time complexity of Selection Sort?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Because Selection Sort uses nested loops to compare elements regardless of initial ordering, its complexity is always O(n^2).

questions.question: How does Insertion Sort build its sorted portion compared to Selection Sort?
options: It picks the absolute minimum and places it at the very end.
It takes one item at a time and inserts it into its correct sorted position among the previously sorted elements.
It splits the array into two equal halves recursively.
It randomly shuffles elements until they are sorted.
questions.explanation: Insertion sort picks the next item and shifts preceding larger items rightward to insert it in its correct position.

questions.question: What is the best-case time complexity of Insertion Sort when the input list is already sorted?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: When data is already sorted, Insertion Sort only makes n-1 comparisons and 0 inner loop shifts, giving O(n) best-case time.

questions.question: What does the "Divide" step mean in a Divide-and-Conquer algorithm?
options: Combining sorted sub-arrays into a single list
Breaking a problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems of the same type
Deleting half of the elements to save memory
Dividing the runtime by the number of processors
questions.explanation: Divide-and-Conquer breaks down complex problems into smaller sub-problems until they are small enough to solve directly.

questions.question: Which programming concept is foundational for implementing Divide-and-Conquer algorithms like Merge Sort?
options: Inheritance
Recursion
Pointers
Infinite loops
questions.explanation: Merge Sort recursively calls itself on the left and right halves of an array until reaching single-element base cases.

questions.question: What are the two main phases of Merge Sort?
options: Scan and Swap
Push and Pop
Divide (split) and Conquer (merge)
Encapsulate and Inherit
questions.explanation: Merge Sort recursively divides the unsorted list into sub-lists until size 1, then merges those sub-lists into a sorted list.

questions.question: How does Merge Sort handle combining two sorted sub-lists into one larger sorted list?
options: It compares the front elements of both sub-lists and repeatedly picks the smaller one to place into a new combined list.
It appends them together and runs Selection Sort on the result.
It discards duplicates and keeps only unique elements.
It sorts them randomly until they fit.
questions.explanation: By comparing the head elements of two already sorted sub-lists, Merge Sort efficiently builds a merged sorted array.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Merge Sort in all cases (Worst, Average, and Best)?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: Merge Sort consistently splits arrays in log(n) levels and performs n work merging per level, yielding O(n log n) across all cases.

questions.question: Why is Merge Sort generally much faster than Selection Sort and Insertion Sort for very large datasets?
options: Because it uses O(1) auxiliary space.
Because its O(n log n) growth rate scales significantly better than O(n^2) as n gets very large.
Because it never uses memory allocations.
Because it skips checking odd-indexed numbers.
questions.explanation: As n grows into thousands or millions of elements, O(n log n) growth rate requires vastly fewer operations than O(n^2).

questions.question: What is a major trade-off or disadvantage of Merge Sort regarding memory usage?
options: It is an in-place algorithm that cannot use extra memory.
It requires extra auxiliary space (out-of-place) to store the split sub-arrays during merging.
It causes memory leaks in Python.
It requires exponential space O(2^n).
questions.explanation: Standard Merge Sort requires O(n) auxiliary space to hold temporary left and right sub-arrays during the merge phase.

questions.question: In recursion, what is the critical condition required to prevent infinite loops and stack overflow?
options: A base case that stops the recursion when a condition is met
A global variable tracking loop counts
A try-except error handler
An iterative loop wrapper
questions.explanation: A base case specifies when the function should return a value without making further recursive calls.

questions.question: If a list has n = 8 elements, how many total comparisons are performed by Selection Sort?
questions.explanation: Using the comparisons formula T(n) = n(n-1)/2: T(8) = (8 * 7) / 2 = 28 comparisons.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm performs the fewest comparisons when given an already sorted list?
options: Selection Sort
Insertion Sort
Both perform the exact same number
Neither can process sorted lists
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort makes only (n-1) comparisons on an already sorted list, whereas Selection Sort still performs n(n-1)/2 comparisons.

questions.question: When choosing between sorting algorithms, which factor determines whether an algorithm is classified as "in-place"?
options: Whether it runs inside a web browser or terminal
Whether it sorts the list using little to no extra memory allocation (O(1) auxiliary space)
Whether it is written in Python or C++
Whether it sorts elements from right to left
questions.explanation: An algorithm is in-place if it modifies the array directly without requiring significant additional memory (O(1) extra space).
